principles.rule: Good design is Easier To Change (ETC). When in doubt, choose the option that keeps future change cheap.
checks: decisions reduce coupling and increase changeability

principles.rule: DRY: every piece of knowledge has a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation. Avoid duplicating knowledge, not just code.
checks: single source of truth for each fact

principles.rule: Keep components orthogonal/decoupled: a change in one area must not ripple into unrelated areas. Apply Tell-Don't-Ask and the Law of Demeter.
Don't program by coincidence: only write code you fully understand; rely on reasons, not luck.
checks: each construct has a known reason

principles.rule: Crash early and use Design by Contract: make pre/postconditions and invariants explicit with assertions; fail fast instead of continuing with a corrupt state.
Don't live with broken windows: fix small defects and bad code as soon as you see them to prevent decay.
checks: no accumulating known defects left untouched in edited code

principles.rule: Prefer tracer bullets: build a thin, working end-to-end skeleton early, then flesh it out. Throw prototypes away after learning from them.
Refactor early and often; treat refactoring as continuous gardening, not a big-bang event.
A test is the first user of your code: write tests to get feedback on design, automate them, and keep them ruthless and continuous.
checks: automated test coverage for important behavior

principles.rule: Name things well and rename when names no longer fit; names carry intent and domain meaning.
Automate everything reproducible and always use version control; do not rely on manual, error-prone procedures.
